newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil prices tick down ahead of OPEC meeting.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil prices tick down ahead of OPEC meeting.

text.p: World oil prices ebbed lower on Friday as the market wound down ahead of a meeting of OPEC ministers in Vienna next week.

With little news to rock the fundamentally bearish tone of the market, prices remained shored up in a tight range, challenged only by selling ahead of the expiry of the July crude futures contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX).
Dealers said trading volume was low as many players, in particular the investment funds, were unwilling to take large positions with the memory of last week's plummet to 13-month lows still fresh.
London August futures for Benchmark Brent Blend crude were 19 cents lower at $17.59 by 1516 GMT. Over the week the price was barely changed.
The expiry of the U.S. July contract prompted a foray below a comfortable trading range established over the previous two days.
And as Brent threatened to revisit its 13-month low of $17.32 a barrel, worries about oversupply persisted.

A projection from the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) headquarters showed that in the remainder of 1997, the 11-member cartel should produce around one million barrels a day more than is needed to supply world demand.
Brokers said the only supporting factor for the market was the continuing prospect of a further delay in crude exports from OPEC-member Iraq.

"The bulls are of course hoping that Iraq can deliver the kind of news they need -- if exports are delayed into July, the lost 600,000 to 800,000 barrels per day is clearly supportive," brokers GNI said in a report.

An Iraqi diplomat said on Wednesday Baghdad would not resume oil sales under the second tranche of a humanitarian agreement with the United Nations until money raised in Iraq's first six months of oil sales had all been spent.
But the fall in prices was indication enough that support from the Iraq/U.N. saga was no longer sufficient to cancel out the bearish supply outlook.
And brokers saw little reprieve in the downward pressure coming from the OPEC meeting which starts next Wednesday.

While a handful of Gulf producers led by Saudi Arabia have maintained spare capacity and quota discipline, others like Venezuela and Nigeria have been pumping at full steam without regard for oil prices.
Market observers said the cartel would probably just "roll over" the current production quota. More important was whether it could bring its quota-busting members into line.

"The key issue is the policy of those countries overproducing in making efforts to curb overproduction rather than the formal quotas themselves," said Peter Davies, chief economist for British Petroleum.
But market players doubted that would come.
"There is an argument for OPEC to consider a more aggresive stance but they probably won't," one trader said.
